title: Lone Tree Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lone Tree wells have a 307-foot median depth; finished well costs model at $21,400-$33,500.
h1: Lone Tree, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Lone Tree means looking past the house and checking the water record. Permits within five miles show a wide range of well depths, with a 307-foot median and records reaching 3,220 feet. Reported yields are stronger than many mountain and fractured-bedrock areas, but the data still varies by aquifer, location, and well construction.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records around Lone Tree, including nearby Meridian, Acres Green, Meridian Village, Grand View Estates, Stepping Stone, and Sierra Ridge. It is a planning reference, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. A driller should review the lot, neighboring wells, permitted use, and local construction conditions before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Lone Tree well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Lone Tree is 307 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 585 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the conditions at a particular property. About 33% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 15% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 29% from 300 to 600 feet, and 24% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest record is 3,220 feet.

These records name the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer most often, along with Lower Dawson and Denver aquifers. All aquifer wells in the dataset are Denver Basin aquifer wells. In Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, depth can change substantially over a short distance. Ask for nearby completed wells before treating a driller's depth allowance as a certainty.

sections.heading: Reported well yields around Lone Tree are generally usable
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.3 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The reported mix is 58% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, with 41% above 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset.

That is useful production for ordinary household planning, but it is not the same as unlimited water. Pump size, storage, pressure equipment, well recovery, and the permitted use all matter. An exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35-gpm exempt-well pumping limit. Confirm the permit before assuming irrigation, livestock, or additional homes are allowed.

sections.heading: Water levels in Lone Tree do not show a simple steady decline
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a 395-foot median, with the middle half from 128 to 778 feet below the surface. Only 119 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited view rather than a complete groundwater trend for Lone Tree.

Measurements by decade vary considerably: the median was 284 feet in the 1970s, 1,150 feet in the 2000s, 415 feet in the 2010s, and 250 feet in the 2020s. The series does not move steadily downward; the 2000s are deepest, followed by shallower reported medians. Differences in location, aquifer, and measurement conditions may explain part of that spread. For a purchase, compare actual neighboring water levels and ask how the well performs during dry periods.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity and recent drilling
sections.html:
Lone Tree's surrounding permit record extends from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. Permits issued by decade were 32 in the 1950s, 61 in the 1960s, 448 in the 1970s, 540 in the 1980s, 394 in the 1990s, 487 in the 2000s, 309 in the 2010s, and 214 in the 2020s. That history gives a buyer a substantial set of nearby records to investigate.

The most active drillers appearing in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J). A permit record is not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability. It is a starting point for checking construction reports, depth, yield, aquifer, and the actual location of comparable wells.

sections.heading: What a new Lone Tree well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 307-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $15,400 to $21,500. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models at about $21,400 to $33,500.

A buyer should use the middle-half depth range of 57 to 585 feet to understand the uncertainty in a bid. A shallow result and a deeper result will not carry the same drilling, casing, pump, trenching, or electrical cost. Request a written scope that identifies what happens if the hole is deeper than expected, the yield is inadequate, or the site needs more difficult access and installation work.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic, and building constraints before closing
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a parcel-specific review. Within about ten miles of Lone Tree, the records include 120 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but it is a reason to check the well location, water testing history, and groundwater direction with qualified professionals.

Low yield and dry-hole risk are not captured by the reported yield percentages alone, because only 713 wells report a pump yield and 1,602 report total depth. Septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway access, grading, and the building envelope can limit a lot before drilling begins. Confirm DWR permitting, water-quality testing, septic design, and any augmentation requirement for the proposed use.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying or building in Lone Tree
sections.html:
Start with wells close to the parcel in Meridian, Acres Green, Meridian Village, Grand View Estates, Stepping Stone, and Sierra Ridge, then separate comparable wells by aquifer, use, depth, and construction date. The local median yield and depth are helpful for budgeting, but they do not replace a site-specific drilling opinion.

For a purchase, make the well permit, construction report, pump information, water test, and legal water use part of due diligence. For a new build, have the driller and septic designer review access, setbacks, storage, electrical service, and the proposed house location together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for the intended use. Colorado DWR can confirm the permit rules before you commit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lone Tree, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within five miles of Lone Tree is 307 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 585 feet, while 24% of reported wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 3,220 feet, so nearby well records matter more than the median alone when estimating a new drilling depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Lone Tree?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 307-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at $15,400 to $21,500. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models at $21,400 to $33,500. Actual pricing depends on depth, access, construction, and the final equipment scope.

faq.q: How much water do Lone Tree wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 13.0-gpm median, with the middle half from 10.3 to 15.0 gpm. About 58% of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gpm and 41% report more than 15 gpm. These figures describe reported wells, not a guarantee for a new hole or a particular property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Lone Tree, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 120 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for relevant contaminants, review its history, and locate nearby environmental sites before relying on the water.

faq.q: Can I use a Lone Tree well for a new home?
faq.a: Possibly, but the permit and proposed use control the answer. Domestic or household wells make up 39% of the local use mix, while irrigation makes up 5%. Colorado rules include a 35-gpm exempt-well pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin. Confirm DWR approval, septic requirements, and water quality before building.
